catan: Buy Seafarers first, since it adds ships and islands without making the game much heavier. Skip the 5-6 player extensions unless five or six people actually show up, or you will own half a pair of shoes.
7-wonders: Buy 7 Wonders: Cities (2nd Edition) first, as it is widely called one of the best. Stay with the 2nd edition, because the publisher warns against mixing editions, and I take warnings seriously.
7-wonders-duel: Pantheon is the one to buy first, said by a reviewer with over a thousand plays to lift the game to among the best for two. Agora can create a runaway leader, which I find oddly relatable.
a-feast-for-odin: The Norwegians goes first, being almost a version 2.0 that rebalances actions without extra complexity. The mini expansions depend on your print, since the renewed base game already includes some of them.
aeons-end: Start with War Eternal, a standalone big box, before any small box. Past and Future is a large campaign box, not a first purchase, however loudly your shelf calls.
agricola: Artifex Deck and Bubulcus Deck come first, since the base game only samples decks A and B. Farmers of the Moor is divisive, so leave it until your fields feel too easy.
anachrony: Fractures of Time is the first purchase, praised for fixing the base game's small flaws. The Infinity Box can be skipped unless you crave the limited-run serial number, which I admit is a niche craving.
architects-of-the-west-kingdom: Age of Artisans comes first, being very easy to integrate. The West Kingdom Tomesaga needs all three West Kingdom games, so it can wait, as can my bank balance.
arcs: Neither expansion is a casual buy, which is refreshing. The Blighted Reach is the bigger one, sprawling with a heavy rules overhead, so it depends on your appetite for campaigns.
ark-nova: Marine Worlds goes first, having won the 2023 Golden Geek Best Expansion award. Zoo Map Pack 1 has only two new layouts, so it suits completists, a breed I know well.
arkham-horror-third-edition: Dead of Night is the one to buy first, since it doubles each neighbourhood encounter deck. Two Secrets of the Order scenarios are among the hardest, so choose according to your tolerance for being gently devoured.
arkham-horror-the-card-game: The Edge of the Earth Investigator Expansion tops the list for card pool building. The Edge of the Earth Campaign is bookkeeping-heavy and a poor first campaign, much like my tax returns.
azul: There is exactly one expansion, so Crystal Mosaic it is, mercifully. Opinions range from must-have to a rating of 3, and you need the original Azul first.
bang: Dodge City is the first buy, the most-rated expansion and the way to reach 8 players. Several others depend on taste and the evidence for them is thin, so tread carefully.
betrayal-at-house-on-the-hill: There is no single first buy, because it hinges on your edition. Widow's Walk needs the 2nd edition, and The Yuletide Tale is the lowest rated, so buy it only if a holiday haunting delights you.
blood-rage: Mystics of Midgard heads the list, though some say it adds little. Gods of Asgard splits opinion, so save it for experienced groups and perhaps a quieter Viking afternoon.
carcassonne: Inns & Cathedrals is the first expansion to buy, adding a sixth player without changing the feel. The rest depend on temperament, and I suspect mine is the chaotic kind.
cascadia: A single expansion and a blessedly easy choice: Landmarks. It is not needed for your first games, so play the base game until you are certain, then indulge.
caverna: The Forgotten Folk is the one to buy first, the best large expansion at 8.22 on BGG. Skip Frantic Fiends unless you want it punishing, though some of us find ordinary farming punishing enough.
clank: Sunken Treasures comes first, as several players said to get this if you get only one. The Mummy's Curse can wait because its mummy rarely does much, rather like some of my relatives.
clank-catacombs: Lairs & Lost Chambers is the more sensible first purchase, though reviews are mixed. Underworld adds the most rules overhead and table space, so it depends on how much of your table you love.
concordia: Salsa goes first, the most-recommended pick in buy-order threads. Skip Venus if you play 3-5 without teams, and Solitaria if you never play alone, a confession I would rather not make.
cosmic-encounter: Cosmic Incursion is the easy first buy, adding a sixth player and a Reward deck. Cosmic Alliance hinges on your table size, as most things in life eventually do.
coup: Coup has one expansion, Reformation, and a BGG thread calls the pair the complete game, so buying it first is hardly agonising. There is nothing to skip, which is rare and rather restful.
cthulhu-death-may-die: Fear of the Unknown is the first addition, named best by most posters in a March 2025 BGG thread. The Unspeakable Box's Lost Episodes are rated mixed, so approach them as one approaches a damp cellar.
decrypto: Laserdrive is the only Decrypto expansion, so buy it first and last, if at all. It rates 7.48 on BGG, though one group dropped it for forcing themed clues.
disney-villainous: Evil Comes Prepared is the one to buy first, since Wargamer names it best for beginners and every box mixes with the others. Skip Despicable Plots to begin with, as it is fiddly.
dixit: Dixit: Quest goes in the basket first, being from the base game's own artist and slipping in unnoticed. Memories and Mirrors can wait, and everything needs a base game, so check the shelf before the wallet.
dominion: With fifteen expansions, roughly fourteen more than anyone needs, begin with Seaside, the set most guides name as the best first one. Prosperity and Menagerie can follow if the habit takes hold.
dune-imperium: Rise of Ix is the one most BGG repliers picked to get first, thanks to new leaders and tech tiles. Skip Uprising if the base plus Rise of Ix pleases you, as it is a second full game.
earth: There are only two Earth expansions, which makes choosing mercifully simple: Abundance goes first, rated 8.06 on BGG. Animal Kingdom comes later, and only if you can tolerate some unbalanced animal powers.
eclipse-second-dawn-for-the-galaxy: Start with the Turn Order Variant, which a BGG poster lists as the first must have and which you can apparently print yourself, if feeling thrifty. The rest depend on whether your group has 24 plays behind it.
eldritch-horror: Forsaken Lore is what BGG regulars call the only must-have, filling the base game out to what it should have been. After that, the small boxes are the best value, and the cosmos can wait.
everdell: Everdell Newleaf is the safe first purchase, more of the same game done well, and ranked best boxed expansion by Meeple Mountain. Bellfaire matters only at five or six players, so resist the urge to buy everything.
exploding-kittens: Streaking Kittens is the one two BGG players pick when told to buy just one, and one calls the base game close to unplayable without it, which seems harsh. Barking Kittens comes second, and languages must match.
five-tribes: The Artisans of Naqala is the first expansion to buy, rated 8.12 on BGG, though posters warn it is out of print and hard to find. The Thieves of Naqala is minor, so leave it until last.
flash-point-fire-rescue: Extreme Danger is the one to buy first, being the only expansion that mixes with earlier maps and, usefully, the storage box for the rest. Skip Tragic Events until veterans arrive, as it makes games about 50% longer.
forest-shuffle: Alpine is the first purchase, rated 8.2 from 3,642 ratings and shuffled straight into the deck. Skip Exploration unless solo mode, caves and promo cards sound like you.
gaia-project: Gaia Project has only one official expansion, The Lost Fleet, which makes this the shortest shopping list in the hobby. A BGG reviewer who loves the base game says it never needed one, so it is for long-time fans.
gloomhaven: Forgotten Circles is our top pick, though it is rather like buying dessert after the funeral, since it is best saved for after the campaign. Irritable Enchanter is the one reviewers praise.
great-western-trail: Rails to the North (2nd Edition) is the one to buy first if you own the 2nd Edition base and play repeatedly, since opinion is split but mostly positive. The 1st Edition box suits only 1st-edition owners.
heat-pedal-to-the-metal: Heavy Rain is the one to buy first, since most replies in BGG's which-expansion thread chose it, and puddles are easy to grasp. Tunnel Vision comes second, and Legends matters only if you race against bots.
here-to-slay: Here to Slay has no clear winner, but Berserkers & Necromancers, at 7.51 from 760 ratings, edges out Warriors & Druids as the one to open with. The Kickstarter-exclusive sets mean a secondary-market hunt.
hero-realms: Begin with Character Pack: Cleric, which a BGG poster calls the most straightforward for younger or newer players. The Ancestry pack is the best of the small packs, adding flavour without complexity.
heroquest: Kellar's Keep is what Blue Dragon Board Games calls the best first expansion, a seamless continuation at medium difficulty. The Mage of the Mirror is difficult, so wait for seasoned heroes.
istanbul: There are just two Istanbul expansions, so Mocha & Baksheesh comes first, with a BGG poster saying that if you buy only one, buy this. Owners call both fun spice rather than necessary, which saves some money.
its-a-wonderful-world: Corruption & Ascension is the one to buy first, rated 8.12 from 2,111 ratings, and some BGG owners will not play without it. Leisure & Decadence divides owners, so approach with caution.
king-of-tokyo: Power Up is the community pick for the first expansion, and getting it early matters because the Evolution cards in the Halloween, King Kong and Cthulhu sets need it. Skip Baby Gigazaur, which adds no new rules.
legendary-a-marvel-deck-building-game: With 33 expansions, Legendary resembles a small continent, so begin with Dark City, which a BGG blog ranks first as the set that completes the base game. X-Men is crushingly difficult, so approach it with a clear head.
lords-of-waterdeep: There is only one expansion here, Scoundrels of Skullport, so the decision is blissfully short. Owners called it pretty fun, though another warned it will not please everyone, so check your group's appetite for complication.
lost-ruins-of-arnak: Buy Expedition Leaders first, which adds variety without upsetting the game, rather like a new hat. Twisted Paths can wait until you own an earlier expansion.
mage-knight-board-game: Mage Knight lets you spend an evening wandering a map and still feel behind schedule. Buy The Lost Legion first, which fixes the ranged-attack and block balance, and eye Shades of Tezla warily.
mansions-of-madness: Buying into Mansions of Madness resembles renting a haunted house, so choose carefully. Streets of Arkham is the first big box to buy, and Path of the Serpent is best saved for last.
marvel-champions: Choosing among Marvel Champions boxes feels like picking a favourite grandchild. Buy NeXt Evolution first, and leave Age of Apocalypse until you own a few expansions.
marvel-united: Marvel United has 23 expansions, roughly 22 more than any sensible shelf holds. Buy Return of the Sinister Six first, with seven villains, and remember each one needs a core box.
memoir-44: Memoir '44 invites you to buy an entire war, one cardboard theater at a time. Redditors name Eastern Front as the first army pack, and Tigers in the Snow can wait.
munchkin: Nobody has ever been seen finishing a Munchkin collection, so start sensibly with Munchkin 2: Unnatural Axe. Its cards simply mix into the base deck, which is more than most relationships manage.
mysterium: Mysterium has only two expansions, a pleasantly short decision in this hobby. Buy Secrets & Lies first, and treat Hidden Signs as variety that matters less.
nemesis: Nemesis already tries to kill you, so adding more seems optimistic. Aftermath is the one most owners call worth it, though several say the Epilogue mode rarely gets played.
obsession: Obsession is about Victorian estates, and its expansions deserve similar restraint. Buy Upstairs, Downstairs first, and file the Characters Expansion under maybe, since owners are divided.
orleans: Orléans can happily go without expansions, and a few players say so. If you must spend, Trade & Intrigue is the first buy, with Invasion for co-op and solo fans.
pandemic: Pandemic expansions arrive in a sensible order, which is more than most outbreaks manage. Buy On the Brink first, since the extra roles alone are worth it, and leave State of Emergency until last.
power-grid: Power Grid has so many maps that one suspects electricity was never the point. Buy Benelux / Central Europe Recharged first, and keep Korea / China Recharged for experienced groups, since China is brutally scarce.
race-for-the-galaxy: Race for the Galaxy expansions come in arcs, and mixing them tests friendships. Buy The Gathering Storm first, and keep Alien Artifacts and Xeno Invasion in their own arcs.
raiders-of-the-north-sea: Raiders of the North Sea has three expansions, two fewer than the Vikings usually required. Hall of Heroes is the one to buy first, though Garphill lists it as out of stock.
robinson-crusoe: Robinson Crusoe is about being stranded, so the sensible response is buying little. Treasure Chest is the better first purchase, and Mystery Tales, with about 20 more rule pages, suits veterans.
roll-player: Roll Player has only two expansions, so the shopping list is mercifully brief. Buy Monsters & Minions first, which owners call the full game, and consider Fiends & Familiars only if you like gambling.
root: Root has a dozen or so expansions, all woodland creatures with ambitions. Buy The Exiles and Partisans Deck first, since it is cheap and easy to add, and the Homeland Expansion after it.
sagrada: Sagrada is about stained glass, so its expansions are partly a question of glitter. Panorama is the first box if you ever have more than four players, and the 2025 Promo Pack is skippable.
scythe: Scythe expansions are best approached like a large dinner, in the right order. Start with The Rise of Fenris, then leave Invaders from Afar unless you often have 6 to 7 players.
seti-search-for-extraterrestrial-intelli: SETI has exactly one expansion, the easiest recommendation in the galaxy. Buy Space Agencies, rated 8.85 against 8.41 for the base game, though some find the organizations forgettable.
small-world: Small World has so many races that a fantasy kingdom would surely collapse from overcrowding. Buy Sky Islands first, and take one Power Pack after the other or instead of it.
smash-up: Smash Up has twelve expansions, about eleven more than a table can absorb. Awesome Level 9000 is the first pick, and 3 to 4 players need a second set.
space-base: Space Base has six expansions, a few with the faint smell of homework. Buy Genesis first, and skip The Mysteries of Terra Proxima until you have played the base game many times.
spirit-island: Spirit Island rewards patience, so take its expansions in modest sips. Branch & Claw is the small, cheap first step, and Nature Incarnate should come last.
splendor: Splendor has two expansions, so the agonizing ends before lunch. Buy The Silk Road first, which reviewers call variety without added complexity; The Sun Never Sets can wait, since it brings more to think about.
star-realms: Choosing among Star Realms expansions is like picking one star from the Milky Way, so grab Crisis - Bases & Battleships first. Fleets & Fortresses is much the same, and every pack needs a core set.
star-wars-imperial-assault: Heart of the Empire is the one to buy first, a tougher Rebel campaign that owners praise with the warmth usually reserved for pets. Jabba's Realm and Return to Hoth can wait their turn.
star-wars-rebellion: The shopping list here is refreshingly short: Rise of the Empire. Many owners say they would not play without it, though a few stubbornly prefer base combat, and it needs the base game, naturally.
takenoko: Takenoko's advice is mercifully brief: buy Chibis. Several owners say it cuts the base game's luck, which is remarkable for a panda, but the tiles do not fit the Collector's Edition.
talisman: Start with The Reaper, the most-rated expansion, which one poster thinks could have lived in the base game. The corner boards are worth it too, though The City is more shopping trip than adventure.
tapestry: Arts & Architecture is the first purchase, the only expansion that actually changes play, easing crowding at four and five players. The Revised Civilization Pack is a skip if your box already carries the revised banner.
terra-mystica: Fire & Ice is the one to buy first, praised as pretty much the best of all possible Terra Mystica worlds, which is a lot to ask of cardboard. Merchants of the Seas is heavier than the base game.
terraforming-mars: Prelude comes first, since both rankings put it there and it cuts the slow opening rounds with almost no new rules. Venus Next lengthens games, so skip it if yours already run long.
terraforming-mars-ares-expedition: Discovery is the first buy, called the most highly recommended expansion for solo and two players by one poster. Crisis suits co-op groups only, and Foundations is for five or six players.
castles-of-burgundy: No box carries a buy-first stamp, so Vineyard leads the list, though it comes with hefty rules overhead and exists only in the Special Edition. Trade Routes is the easy addition owners always play with.
the-isle-of-cats: Kittens + Beasts is the first purchase, called the only expansion that changes gameplay, though one poster found its events too abstract. The Boat Pack adds no rule changes, and Late Arrivals matters only at five or six players.
journeys-in-middle-earth: Shadowed Paths is the one to buy first, since the base game offers only two campaigns and few heroes, and this addresses both complaints. Spreading War is a second big campaign, best taken afterward.
the-lord-of-the-rings-the-card-game: The Dark of Mirkwood Scenario is a sensible first purchase, the cheapest way to add quests after the Revised Core Set. Dream-Chaser is the most mechanically complex campaign, so wait until you are confident or merely stubborn.
the-quacks-of-quedlinburg: The Herb Witches is the one to buy first, with most replies picking it for the fifth player and saying it barely adds complexity. The Alchemists needs a conversation, since posters say it bloats a light game.
the-quest-for-el-dorado: Dangers & Muisca leads the way, since one poster says it changes card values and enables varied maps. Heroes & Hexes needs the Caves variant, and the curse tokens earned a poster's scorn.
the-resistance: Hidden Agenda should be bought first, the highest rated of the three, with posters calling its Assassin roles must-have. Posters split on the plot cards, which is a fair summary of most conspiracies.
ticket-to-ride: Start with Map Collection Vol. 7: Japan & Italy, called a fan favorite and a perfect place to begin. USA 1910 works only with the original USA box, so check your shelf first.
too-many-bones: The best first purchase is 40 Days in Daelore, the most-rated content pack, adding 40 encounters and 15 Baddies. Rage of Tyranny is for groups that already beat the base game, which is honest and slightly alarming.
twilight-imperium: There are only two expansions, and Prophecy of Kings is the first, treated by regular groups as the default way to play. Thunder's Edge is wilder, rather like inviting a loud cousin to a quiet dinner.
unstable-unicorns: No expansion gets a buy-first stamp, so Nightmares tops the list, the highest score among full 54-card packs, with no new rules to teach. Rainbow Apocalypse stretches playtime too much, according to posters.
viticulture-essential-edition: Tuscany Essential Edition is the one to buy first, called a must-have by reviewers for its four-season board and new actions without much extra time. Viticulture World is a hard co-op mode for strong players only.
war-of-the-ring: Lords of Middle-earth leads the list, but a Reddit thread says neither it nor Warriors is required, and suggests waiting until after many plays. Warriors drew lukewarm remarks, one commenter calling it bloat.
wingspan: Oceania is the expansion most reviewers say to get first, as its new mats and nectar change the game more than any other box. Asia is a depends pick, since reviewers call its 6-7 player mode messy.
wyrmspan: Wyrmspan has exactly one expansion, so the shopping list is pleasantly short: Dragon Academy. Two reviews like the round tracker, though a 70-play poster finds hatchlings less useful, so even dragons have critics.
